## Overview

A survival time is *left censored* when the event is known to have happened
already by the time the subject is first examined, but not when.  All that is
recorded is an upper bound $t_R$: the event occurred somewhere in $(0, t_R]$.
This arises whenever the outcome is detected by inspection rather than observed
as it happens - a tumour already present at the first scan, seroconversion
already complete at enrolment, a milestone already reached at the first
assessment.

The likelihood contribution is the distribution function rather than the
survivor function,

$$P(T \leq t_R) = 1 - S(t_R) = 1 - \exp\bigl\{-H_0(t_R)e^{\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\beta}}\bigr\},$$

which the partial likelihood cannot accommodate: it needs a risk set at a known
event time, and a left-censored subject supplies neither.  Because
`coxph_mpl()` estimates $H_0$ explicitly, left-censored observations enter the
likelihood directly, and may be mixed freely with exact events and right- and
interval-censored observations in the same fit.

## Encoding left-censored observations

Left censoring uses the `type = "interval2"` response, with `NA` in place of the
unknown lower endpoint:

```{r encoding}
library(survivalMPL)
library(survival)

Surv(c(NA, 2, 3, 5), c(7, 4, NA, 5), type = "interval2")
```

The four observations above are, in order: left censored at 7 (`7-`), interval
censored on $(2, 4]$, right censored at 3 (`3+`), and an exact event at 5.
`Surv()` records the distinction in its status code, and `coxph_mpl()` dispatches
on that code:

```{r status-codes}
s <- Surv(c(NA, 2, 3, 5), c(7, 4, NA, 5), type = "interval2")
data.frame(status = s[, 3],
           meaning = c("left censored", "interval censored",
                       "right censored", "exact event"))
```

Note that `NA` here is *information*, not missingness: these rows are kept, not
dropped by `na.action`.

Recording a left-censored observation as `NA` and recording it as the interval
$(0, t_R]$ describe the same event, since $S(0) = 1$ makes $1 - S(t_R)$ and
$S(0) - S(t_R)$ identical.  Both encodings are accepted; the `NA` form is the
one that states the intent.

---

## Example: HIV seroconversion in people who inject drugs

The example uses `drugusers` from the CRAN package **icpack** [@Gomez2000]:
940 people who inject drugs, attending a hospital detoxification unit in
Barcelona, followed for HIV seroconversion.  The data are not bundled with
survivalMPL, so the code below runs only when icpack is installed.

```{r icpack-check, include=FALSE}
have_icpack <- requireNamespace("icpack", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = have_icpack)
```

```{r icpack-missing, echo=FALSE, eval=!have_icpack, results="asis"}
cat("> **Note.** The icpack package is not installed, so the code in this",
    "section was not run. Install it with `install.packages(\"icpack\")`.")
```

Time is measured from the start of injecting drug use, and HIV status is only
known at test visits.  That gives all four observation types:

- the first test was already positive: seroconversion happened somewhere in
  $(0, t_R]$ - **left censored**;
- a negative test followed by a positive one: seroconversion lies between the
  two - **interval censored**;
- the last test was negative: **right censored**;
- the two tests coincide: an **exact** time.

In `drugusers`, `left` is the last negative test (0 if the first test was
already positive) and `right` the first positive test (`Inf` if the last test
was negative), both in months.  Converting to years and replacing the open
bounds by `NA` gives the encoding described above:

```{r hiv-data}
data(drugusers, package = "icpack")

ivdu <- data.frame(
  t_L         = ifelse(drugusers$left == 0, NA, drugusers$left / 12),
  t_R         = ifelse(is.finite(drugusers$right), drugusers$right / 12, NA),
  Female      = as.integer(drugusers$gender == "female"),
  Age_centred = (drugusers$age - mean(drugusers$age)) / 10,
  period      = relevel(factor(as.character(drugusers$period)), "1972-1980")
)

table(status = Surv(ivdu$t_L, ivdu$t_R, type = "interval2")[, 3])
```

Status `2` marks the 530 left-censored subjects, more than half the sample,
status `3` the 65 interval-censored ones, status `0` the 343 right-censored
ones and status `1` the 2 exact times.  `Age_centred` is age at the start of
drug use in decades, centred at the sample mean, and `period` is the period in
which drug use began, with 1972-1980 as the reference.

### Model fit

$H_0$ is evaluated at $t_R$ for every left-censored subject, so the shape of the
baseline matters more here than it does for right-censored data.  That argues
for a smooth basis, `basis = "msplines"`.  Everything else, including the
automatic selection of the smoothing value, is left at its default; `tol` is
loosened to `1e-05`, as in the other articles - see **Control Parameters**.

```{r hiv-fit}
fit_hiv <- coxph_mpl(
  Surv(t_L, t_R, type = "interval2") ~ Female + Age_centred + period,
  data  = ivdu,
  basis = "msplines",
  tol   = 1e-05
)

summary(fit_hiv)
```

The summary counts only the 2 exact times as "events"; the other 938 subjects
enter the likelihood through censored contributions.  Hazard ratios with 95%
confidence intervals are easier to read:

```{r hiv-hr}
est <- coef(fit_hiv)
se  <- fit_hiv$se$Beta$M2HM2

round(cbind(HR    = exp(est),
            lower = exp(est - 1.96 * se),
            upper = exp(est + 1.96 * se)), 2)
```

Women seroconvert faster than men at the same age and period, by about a
quarter.  The hazard is lower for those who began injecting later, 22% lower
in 1986-1991 and 31% lower in 1992-1997 than in 1972-1980, though only the
first of these comes close to significance, and the confidence intervals are
wide.  Age at initiation has no detectable effect.  Real data come with no
known truth to compare against, so the check is robustness: the coefficients
barely move when the basis is changed.

```{r hiv-robust}
fit_unif <- coxph_mpl(
  Surv(t_L, t_R, type = "interval2") ~ Female + Age_centred + period,
  data  = ivdu,
  basis = "uniform",
  tol   = 1e-05
)

round(cbind(msplines = coef(fit_hiv), uniform = coef(fit_unif)), 3)
```

### Baseline hazard and survival

```{r hiv-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(fit_hiv, ask = FALSE, cex.main = 0.8)
```

The four panels are the M-spline basis functions, then the estimated baseline
hazard, cumulative hazard and survival.  The hazard panel is the one to read
first: the risk of seroconversion is highest soon after drug use begins and
declines with its duration.  The estimate is close to a straight line because the
automatic smoothing value is very large; the confidence band is wide, and
honestly so, since a left-censored subject only says that the event happened at
some point before $t_R$.

```{r hiv-hazard, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.5}
plot(fit_hiv, which = 2, ask = FALSE, cex.main = 0.9)
```

### Predicted survival

Because $H_0$ is estimated, survival can be predicted for a named covariate
profile rather than only compared between profiles.  Here are a woman and a
man who began injecting in the same period at the same age:

```{r hiv-predict, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.5}
i_f <- which(ivdu$Female == 1 & ivdu$period == "1981-1985" &
             drugusers$age == 19)[1]
i_m <- which(ivdu$Female == 0 & ivdu$period == "1981-1985" &
             drugusers$age == 19)[1]

p_f <- predict(fit_hiv, type = "survival", i = i_f)
p_m <- predict(fit_hiv, type = "survival", i = i_m)

par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 3, 1))
plot(p_m$time, p_m$survival, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2.4,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Years since first injecting drug use",
     ylab = expression(hat(S)(t)), las = 1,
     main = "Predicted survival free of seroconversion", cex.main = 0.95)
lines(p_f$time, p_f$survival, col = "tomato", lwd = 2.4)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("man", "woman"),
       col = c("steelblue", "tomato"), lwd = 2.4, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

## Next steps

- **Interval Censoring** covers the general partly interval-censored case, of
  which left censoring is the boundary instance, and uses a dataset containing
  all four observation types at once.
- **Right Censoring** covers the standard scheme and the `Surv(time, status)`
  response.
- **Control Parameters** explains `n.knots`, `basis` and `smooth`, the settings
  that decide how much structure the baseline hazard is allowed to have.
- **Basis Functions for the Baseline Hazard** explains the choice of $\psi_u$;
  because $H_0(t_R)$ enters the left-censored likelihood directly, that choice
  matters more here than for right-censored data alone.
